ἐροῦμεν πρὸς ταῦτα; εἰ ὁ θεὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, τίς καθ' ἡμῶν; ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ
ἐφείσατο, ἀλλ' ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν παρέδωκεν αὐτόν, πῶς οὐχὶ καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ χαρίσεται ἡμῖν
τὰ πάντα; ὥσπερ ἀνακ<ε>φαλαιούμενος τὰ προειρημένα καὶ ἐπ' ἐκεῖνα ἀναφέρων
ταῦτά φησιν, οὐ παρὰ τὸ ἐναργὲς λέγων. ἑώρα γὰρ κατὰ τὸ καὶ ἔ ε θε μ(ι) ούμενοι
ὑπὸ πάντων διὰ τὸ ὄνομά μου ὡς πολλοὶ καθ' ἡμῶν, καὶ οὐ μόνον ἄνθρωποι ἀλλὰ
καὶ τὰ πρὸς ἃ ἡ πάλη, ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξου ίαι καὶ κο μοκράτορε τοῦ κότου τούτου καὶ τὰ
πνευματικὰ τῆ πονηρία ἐν τοῖ ἐπουρανίοι καὶ αὐτὸς ὅλος ὁ πλεονεκτεῖν ἡμᾶς
θέλων Σατανᾶ · μὴ παρὰ τὸ ἐναργὲς δὲ λέγων τὸ εἰ ὁ θεὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, εὐτελὴς καὶ
οὐδενὸς λόγου ἄξιός ἐστιν καὶ οὐδὲν δυνάμενος ἕκαστος τῶν καθ' ἡμῶν· μὴ οὖν
εὐλαβεῖσθε μηδὲ ταράσσεσθε· εἰ μὲν γὰρ μόνοι ἦτε καὶ μὴ μετὰ θεοῦ πρὸς τοιούτους
ἀνθιστάμενοι, κἂν εὔλογόν τι ἔχειν ἐδοκεῖτε φοβεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς· νυνὶ δὲ θεοῦ ὄντος
ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, εἰς τίνα μετρηθήσεται τὰ τοσαῦτα καθ' ἡμῶν ἢ εἰς οὐδέν; 50 viii 33 τίς
ἐγκαλέσει κατὰ ἐκλεκτῶν θεοῦ; θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν· τίς ὁ κατα κρίνων; δοκεῖ μοι τοῦτο
ἀναφέρεσθαι ἐπὶ τὸν διάβολον ὄντα κατήγορον καὶ τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν οἷς ἐγκαλέσει·
οὐδεὶς γάρ ἐστιν οὗ ἐκεῖνος μὴ κατηγορήσει καὶ ᾧ οὐκ ἐγκαλέσει, εἰ μὴ μόνος
Ἰησοῦς, ὃ ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἐποίη εν, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο λέγων νῦν ἔρχεται ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ
κό μου τούτου καὶ ἐν ἐμοὶ οὐκ ἔχει οὐδέν. διὰ τοῦτο οὖν ἐκεῖνος ἐξευτελίζεται
ἐγκαλῶν καὶ κατὰ ἐκλεκτῶν θεοῦ· τοῦ γὰρ θεοῦ δικαιοῦντος τίς κατακρίναι
δύναται, κἂν ὁ κατήγορος φέρει εἰς μέσον τὰ ἀπηλιμμένα ἐφ' οἷς κατεκρίθησαν εἰ μὴ
ἀπήλιπτο; ἐδικαίωσεν δὲ αὐτοὺς ὡ νεφέλην ἀπαλείψα τὰ ἀνομία αὐτῶν καὶ ὡ
γνόφον τὰ ἁμαρτία αὐτῶν καὶ λευκάνα τοὺς πρότερον ἡμαρτηκότας ὡ xiόνα. 51
viii 37 ἀλλ' ἐν τούτοις πᾶσιν ὑπερνικῶμεν διὰ τοῦ ἀγαπήσαντος ἡμᾶς. νικᾷ μὲν ὁ
μετὰ ἀμφηρίστου ἀγῶνος τοὺς ἐν τοῖς ἀγωνιζομένοις περὶ νίκης περιγενόμενος τοῦ
ἀνταγωνιστοῦ· ὑπερνικᾷ δὲ ὁ μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπιτρέψας στῆναι πρὸς αὐτὸν τῷ
ἐναντιουμένῳ. τοιοῦτος ὁ Παῦλος καὶ οἱ τὴν ὁμοίαν αὐτῷ παρασκευὴν πρὸς τοὺς
πειρασμοὺς ἀνειληφότες, τὸ θλίβον καταπατοῦντες καὶ ἐντρυφῶντες τῷ
τενοχωροῦντι καὶ τὸ διῶκον τῇ ὑπομονῇ διώκοντες, καὶ τὸν λιμὸν διὰ τὴν
οὐράνιον τροφὴν γελῶντες, καὶ τὴν γυμνότητα ἐν οὐδενὶ τιθέμενοι δι' ὃν
ἐνδέδυνται Χριστόν, καὶ τὸν κίνδυνον ὡς οὐ κινδυνεύοντες καταπατοῦντες, καὶ τὴν
μάχαιραν διὰ τὸν ζῶντα τοῦ θεοῦ λόγον οὐδὲν χαλεπὸν ἐργάσασθαι αὐτοὺς
πειθόμενοι. 52 viii 38, 39 πέπεισμαι γὰρ ὅτι οὔτε θάνατος οὔτε ζωὴ οὔτε ἄγγελοι οὔτε
ἀρχαὶ οὔτε δυνάμεις οὔτε ἐνεστῶτα οὔτε μέλλοντα οὔτε ὕψωμα οὔτε βάθος οὔτε τις
κτίσις ἑτέρα δυνήσεται ἡμᾶς χωρίσαι ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ
τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν. ὅρα εἰ μὴ εὐλόγως τὸ μὲν πέπεισμαι ὅτι οὐ δύναται ἡμᾶς χωρίσαι
τάδε τινὰ ἔταξεν ἐπὶ τῶν μειζόνων ἢ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον πειρα μῶν, τὸ δὲ τί ἡμᾶ
χωρί ει ἐξευτελίζων τοὺς ἀνθρωπίνου ἐπὶ τῶν ἐλαττόνων γυμνασίων τῆς
ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς· καὶ ἐὰν ὑπερνικῶμεν δὲ τὰ πρότερα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα, οὐ χωρὶς
συμπνοίας καὶ ἐνεργείας κρείττονος αὐτῶν περιεσόμεθα· διὸ καλῶς ὁ Παῦλος
προσέθηκεν τὸ διὰ τοῦ ἀγαπή αντο ἡμᾶ . πρόσχες δὲ εἰ θάνατος μὲν παλαίει
βουλόμενος χωρίσαι ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ οὐχ ὁ κοινὸς
περὶ οὗ ἀνωτέρω εἴρηται τὸ ἕνεκέν ου θανατούμεθα ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν, ἀλλ' ὁ ἐχθρὸ
Χριστοῦ καὶ ἔ χατο καταργηθη όμενο · βουλήσεται μὲν γὰρ οὗτος χωρίσαι, φέρε
εἰπεῖν, Παῦλον, οὐ δυνήσεται δὲ καταργούμενο ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ Χριστοῦ· ζωὴ δὲ
οὐχ <ἡ> τῷ θανάτῳ τούτῳ ἐναντία, τὰ γὰρ ἀλλήλοις ἐναντία οὐ πέφυκεν ἓν καὶ
ταὐτὸν βούλεσθαι, ἀλλὰ ἡ καθ' ἣν ζῇ τις τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ καὶ τοῖς εἴδεσιν αὐτῆς καὶ τῷ
ψεύδει· εἰ δὲ καὶ καθ' ἕκαστον εἶδος ἁμαρτία ἔστι τις φαύλῃ ζωῇ, ἐπιστήσεις διὰ τὸ
κρεῖττον τὸ ἔλεό ου ὑπὲρ ζωά · αὕτη γὰρ βουλήσεται μὲν χωρίσαι τὸν ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ
τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, οὐ δύναται δέ, καταργουμένη πῇ μὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ θανάτου
καθ' ὃν ἀποθνή κει τις τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, πῇ δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς ζωῆς ἡμῶν ἥτις κέκρυπται ὺν τῷ
Χρι τῷ ἐν τῷ θεῷ. καὶ ἄγγελοι δὲ βούλονται ἡμᾶς χωρίσαι τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, περὶ ὧν λέλεκται τοῖ ἐξ εὐωνύμων Ὑπάγετε εἰ τὸ πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον
τὸ ἡτοιμα μένον τῷ διαβόλῳ καὶ τοῖ ἀγγέλοι αὐτοῦ. τὸ δὲ οὔτε ἀρχαὶ ἐπὶ τὸ οὐκ
ἐ τὶν ἡμῖν ἡ παλὴ πρὸ αἷμα καὶ άρκα ἀλλὰ πρὸ τὰ ἀρχὰ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς ἀναφέρεται,
pass_a_gloss: What shall we say then? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? As one summing up what has been said before and referring back to these things, he speaks not contrary to the evident facts. For I saw also, according to the and you are being we are by all on account of my name as many against us, and not only men but also the things against which the struggle, rulers and authorities and powers of the world of this and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places and he himself wholly wanting to prevail over us, Satan; do not speak contrary to the evident facts saying that if God is for us, it is contemptible and worthless of any account and each one of those against us is powerless; therefore do not fear nor be disturbed, for if indeed we were alone and not with God contending against such ones, it might seem reasonable to fear us; but now with God being for us, to what shall these many things against us be measured or to nothing? Who will bring a charge against God's elect? God is the one who justifies; who is the one who condemns? It seems to me this is referred back to the devil being an accuser and of the elect whom he accuses; for there is no one whom he does not accuse and against whom he does not bring a charge, except only Jesus, who committed no sin, and therefore now speaking, the ruler of this world comes and in me he has nothing. Therefore he is brought to nothing by accusing and against God's elect; for since God justifies, who can condemn? Even if the accuser brings forward the things from which they were condemned, if they were not left behind; but he justified them as a cloud wiping away their iniquities and as darkness their sins and whitening those who formerly had sinned like zinc. But in all these things we more than conquer through him who loved us. For he conquers who after a struggle of the contenders in the contests concerning victory having come upon the opponent; but he more than conquers who does not even permit the beginning to take a stand against the opposing one. Such is Paul and those who have received the same preparation against temptations, trampling the oppressive and enjoying the one who narrows and the pursuing one by endurance, and the famine by the heavenly food laughing, and the nakedness in nothing putting on, through whom they have clothed themselves Christ, and the danger as not endangering trampling, and the sword by reason of the living word of God not difficult to work, being persuaded. For I am convinced that neither death nor life nor angels nor rulers nor powers nor things present nor things to come nor height nor depth nor any other creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. See if it is not reasonable that I am convinced that these things cannot separate us, having appointed them upon the greater things or according to human trials, and the thing that separates us, disesteeming the human upon the lesser exercises of the human soul; and if we more than conquer the former and human things, we shall not be without surplus breath and energy of a better sort surrounding them; therefore well did Paul add the through the loving us; but consider if death indeed wanting to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, not the common concerning which it was said above, that we die wholly the day, but the enemy of Christ and he having been destroyed; for this one will want to separate us, to speak, Paul, but he will not be able to be destroyed by the one in him Christ; and life is not contrary to this death, for the things mutually contrary do not naturally both want one and the same thing, but the way by which one lives by sin and its appearances and falsehood; but if also for each kind of sin there is some base life, you will know through the better mercy over lives; for this one will want to separate the one in the love of God in Christ Jesus, but she will not be able, being destroyed in part by the death by which one dies on account of sin, and in part by our life which is hidden in Christ in God. And the angels also want to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, concerning which it has been said to those on the left, Go out, if the fire the eternal prepared for the devil and his angels; and the thing that neither rulers upon what is in us the old blood and barrier but before the rulers and the things following are referred back.
pass_b_english: What can we say in response? If God stands with us, who can stand against us? He who did not withhold his own Son but delivered him for our sake—how could he fail to lavish upon us, together with him, every good thing? This is a recapitulation, a return to what has gone before, and he speaks not in defiance of what is plainly evident. I have seen, moreover, how all things rise against us for the sake of that name—people, yes, but also the very forces that oppose: principalities, powers, world-rulers of this dark age, and the spiritual hosts of wickedness in the heavenly realms, with Satan himself bent on our overthrow. Yet we must not claim, contrary to what is evident, that if God is for us, then his cause is insignificant and we are nothing, or that our adversaries are powerless; to think so would be to invite fear and distress, as if we were left alone to contend with such foes. But now that God is for us, what measure can be taken against this array of opposition? To what shall they be compared—if not to nothing? Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen? God himself, who justifies. Who is there to condemn? It seems clear that this points to the devil, the accuser of the brethren, who charges the elect before God—yet there is not one he accuses who is not also defended, save only Jesus, who knew no sin. And so it is said: the ruler of this world comes, and finds in me nothing to lay hold of. Thus he is brought to nothing by his own accusations against God’s elect, for if God justifies, who can condemn? Even if the accuser produces the very things for which they were once condemned—if they had not been left behind—still, God has justified them: as a cloud sweeps away their iniquities, as darkness is scattered before light, as those once stained by sin are made white like refined zinc. Yet in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For the victor in a contest is not merely the one who, after struggle, overtakes his opponent, but the one who does not even allow the beginning of resistance to take shape. Such was Paul, and such are those who have undergone the same preparation against temptation: they trample oppression, find joy in the one who straitens, pursue the hunter by endurance, laugh at famine through heavenly food, regard nakedness as nothing, having put on Christ through whom they are clothed, treat danger as no danger, and wield the sword not by strength but by the living word of God, which they find easy to wield, being persuaded. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, shall be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Consider whether it is not reasonable that I am convinced of this—having appointed these things to be weighed against greater realities, or measured by human trials—and that the very thing that would separate us is nothing but the esteeming of the lesser exercises of the human soul over the greater. And if we more than conquer the former and the human, we shall not lack a better breath and energy surrounding them; thus it was fitting that Paul added the words 'through him who loved us.' But reflect: if death indeed sought to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, it would not be the common fate of which it was said above—that we die wholly each day—but rather the enemy of Christ, who has been destroyed. For this one would seek to divide us, to speak, Paul—but he shall not be destroyed by the one in whom he dwells, Christ. And life is not contrary to this death, for mutually opposed things do not naturally desire the same end; rather, the way of life through sin, its appearances, and falsehood is what opposes it. But if even for each kind of sin there is some base form of life, you will know this through the superior mercy that extends over life. For this one would seek to separate the one embraced in the love of God in Christ Jesus—but she cannot, being destroyed in part by the death through which one dies on account of sin, and in part by our life, which is hidden in Christ in God. And the angels, too, seek to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, concerning whom it has been said to those on the left: 'Depart, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.' And the thing that neither rulers nor what is in us—the old blood and barrier—can effect, but which, before the rulers and the things that follow, is referred back.

bible_refs.note: What shall we say then? If God is for us, who is against us?
He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all...
Who will bring a charge against God's elect? God is the one who justifies...
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? ...
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
The passage matches Romans 8:31-39 in content and structure, including the rhetorical questions, God's justification, Christ's intercession, and the inseparability from God's love.
